name: Double Yukon (Solitaire)
description: Double Yukon is a massive, two-deck variation of the famous Yukon Solitaire. Unlike Klondike, all 104 cards are dealt into the tableau at once, with no stock or waste pile. The game is known for its 'group move' mechanic, allowing players to move any visible stack of cards regardless of their sequence, provided the base card of the stack fits the alternating-color building rule. This makes Double Yukon a deep, analytical game with high win rates for careful players.

history.origins: Yukon Solitaire originated in the North American West during the late 19th-century gold rush era. The 'Double' variation appeared much later, popularized by digital solitaire suites that offered 104ndcard challenges to seasoned players.
timeline: 1890s: Standard Yukon is played in Yukon Territory mining camps.
1910s: Documented in various North American card game books.
1980s-90s: Double Yukon becomes a popular inclusion in computer solitaire software.
history.cultural: Regarded as a 'thinker's solitaire' because almost every deal is winnable if played perfectly.
history.evolution: The game evolved to remove the randomness of the 'Stock' draw, placing all cards on the table and focusing the challenge on sequence management and uncovering face-down cards.

setup.players: One player only. Double Yukon is a solitaire (patience) game; the player plays alone against the layout, moving cards between tableau columns and to foundations with no opponent or partner.
setup.dealing: Cards are dealt into 10 columns. Column 1 has 5 cards (all face-up). Columns 2 through 10 have 7 to 15 cards respectively, with the last 6 cards in each column always face-up and the underlying cards face-down. There is no stock; all cards are on the table.
setup.equipment: Two card decks, large playing surface.

rules.objective: Move all 104 cards to the 8 foundation piles, building each suit up from Ace to King.
rules.gameplay:
1. Tableau Building: Build down in alternating colors (e.g., a Black 10 on a Red Jack).
2. Group Moves: Any face-up card, along with all cards sitting on top of it, can be moved as a unit. The cards above the base card do NOT need to be in any specific order.
3. Foundations: Build up in suit (A-2-3...K). Once a card is on a foundation, it usually cannot be moved back to the tableau.
keyRules: Only a King (or a group headed by a King) can be moved into an empty tableau space.
Flipping Cards: When a face-down card is exposed by moving the cards above it, flip it over immediately.
With 104 cards, you have 8 Aces and 8 Kings to manage.

strategy.basic: Prioritize uncovering the face-down cards in the rightndmost columns, as they contain the largest stacks of hidden cards.
strategy.intermediate: Empty slots: If you don't have a King to move, do not empty a column. You lose a vital building spot that could be used for lower-rank cards.
strategy.advanced: Look deep into the stacks. Since any group can move, you can often pull a needed 5 from the middle of a messy stack to move it to a 6 elsewhere, provided the 5 is face-up.
tips: Always check if a card can go to a foundation before moving it in the tableau.
If you have a choice of two Red 4s to move onto a Black 5, choose the one that is sitting on top of a face-down card.
